newsitem.title: CANADA: Quebec's Parizeau would have declared independence.
newsitem.headline: Quebec's Parizeau would have declared independence.

text.p: Quebec's then-Premier Jacques Parizeau would have declared the province's independence from Canada days after a separatist win in Quebec's 1995 referendum, according to excerpts published on Wednesday from his upcoming memoirs.

The revelation, excerpted in the French-language Quebec City daily Le Soleil, contradicted promises by Parizeau in the campaign for the Oct. 30, 1995, Quebec referendum, which the separatists lost by less than one percentage point.
Parizeau resigned the day after the referendum, after blaming "money and the ethnics" for the defeat.
During the campaign, Parizeau agreed to wait about a year to negotiate the terms of separation and later declare the French-speaking province's sovereignty.

Le Soleil quoted Parizeau's book "For a Sovereign Quebec", to be published in French next Monday, as saying that Parizeau agreed with France that sovereignty would have to be implemented "in the week or in the 10 days following a majority for the yes."
The French embassy in Ottawa declined comment on Wednesday.
French support would have been a key element in ensuring Quebec's recognition as a sovereign country by other nations such as the United States, Parizeau wrote.

"One week before the referendum, the operation meant to end up with the recognition of Quebec by France had been engaged," he wrote. "The diplomatic preparation of sovereignty would have been key to its realisation if the yes side would have won."

A June 1995 agreement among Parizeau's Parti Quebecois and two allied parties -- including current Quebec Premier Lucien Bouchard's Bloc Quebecois -- stated that negotiations to create an economic agreement with the rest of Canada should last about one year after the referendum.

In a pre-recorded speech that would have been broadcast on referendum night if the separatists had won, Parizeau said: "The sovereignty of Quebec will not be proclaimed right away. It could take a year before then National Assembly makes that proclamation."

Parizeau wrote in his book that "my speeches, that are related to the negotiations with Canada, are written in a way to allow such a declaration of sovereignty. I have never committed myself in public or in private not to call a unilateral declaration of independence."
